In one breath.

A numerical method approaches a root of f of x equals zero through successive estimates. Interval bisection uses a sign changing bracket, linear interpolation uses a secant, and Newton Raphson uses a tangent.
Key ideas.

Opposite endpoint signs prove a root only when the function is continuous throughout the interval. For f of x equals one over x on open square bracket minus one, one close square bracket, the signs differ but x equals zero is a discontinuity and there is no root. A tangent root, such as that of x squared at zero, may show no sign change. An interval can also contain several roots, the test proves existence, not uniqueness.

A root is a value r for which f of r equals zero. Often an exact solution is unavailable or inconvenient, so calculate estimates and check their accuracy. For the methods here, f uses functions from P one and P two, the differentiation needed for Newton Raphson is also from P one and P two.

Interval bisection starts with a is less than b where a continuous f has opposite signs at the endpoints, f of a f of b is less than zero. Calculate m equals open bracket a plus b close bracket over two. If f of m equals zero, stop. Otherwise retain open square bracket a, m close square bracket when f of a f of m is less than zero, retain open square bracket m, b close square bracket when f of m f of b is less than zero. Each step halves the bracket width. The midpoint is an estimate, while the whole bracket gives a useful error bound, its distance from the root is at most half the current width.

Linear interpolation replaces the curve between open bracket a, f of a close bracket and open bracket b, f of b close bracket with a straight line. Its crossing of the x axis is. x equals a minus f of a open bracket b minus a close bracket, all over, f of b minus f of a. This is also called a secant estimate. It uses the sizes as well as the signs of the endpoint values, so it generally differs from the midpoint. If repeating with a bracket, evaluate f of x and replace the endpoint with the same sign as f of x.
Notice that the secant joins two curve points, its axis crossing four over three is an estimate, not a point on the curve.

Newton Raphson starts with a chosen x zero. The tangent to y equals f of x at x n crosses the x axis at the next estimate, x sub n plus one, equals x n minus f of x n, all over, f prime of x n. Differentiate correctly and make sure f prime of x n is not equal to zero. A poor starting value or a very small derivative can make the iterates unreliable. Check each iterate against the equation rather than assuming it converges.
Notice that the tangent uses the slope at x equals one point five, its axis crossing seventeen over twelve supplies the next iterate.
Method.
Rearrange the equation as f of x equals zero and identify the required method and accuracy.
For bisection, show endpoint signs, calculate the midpoint and its sign, then write the new bracket. Repeat until its width meets the required accuracy.
For interpolation, calculate both signed endpoint values, substitute in the secant formula, then check the new function value if another step is needed.
For Newton Raphson, find f prime of x, write the recurrence, substitute the current estimate, and calculate the next one. Repeat and verify stability to the requested decimal places.
Worked example.

Let f of x equals x squared minus two and start from open square bracket one, two close square bracket. Since f of one equals minus one and f of two equals two, a root is bracketed. Bisection gives m equals one point five and f of one point five equals zero point two five, so the new bracket is open square bracket one, one point five close square bracket. Linear interpolation from the original endpoints gives x equals one minus open bracket minus one close bracket open bracket two minus one close bracket over open bracket two minus open bracket minus one close bracket close bracket equals four over three. For Newton Raphson, f prime of x equals two x. Starting at x zero equals one point five gives x one equals one point five minus zero point two five over three equals seventeen over twelve is approximately one point four one six seven. These are estimates made by different geometric rules. Substituting each into f checks how close it is to zero.
Traps.

Trap, Keep the half with the smaller endpoint value in bisection. Why it's wrong, The root is identified by a sign change, not a magnitude comparison. Instead, State the signs at both ends of the retained bracket.
Trap, Treat interpolation as another midpoint calculation. Why it's wrong, The secant crosses the axis according to its endpoint heights. Instead, Substitute the signed values in the secant formula.
Trap, Reverse the Newton Raphson quotient. Why it's wrong, The tangent's horizontal correction is function value divided by gradient. Instead, Write f of x n over f prime of x n before substituting.
Exam technique.

For Calculate or Find, show the formula, substitution and estimate. For Show that, include the signs or algebra that justify the stated result. If asked to give an answer to a stated number of decimal places, retain extra figures in intermediate steps and confirm the final rounding using a sufficiently narrow bracket or stable iterates. State when an iterate is undefined because its derivative is zero.

A bracket gives two bounds, an approximation gives one value, often the midpoint. After n bisections, the width is open bracket b minus a close bracket over two to the n, choose the smallest integer n meeting the target width. Stable Newton iterates suggest convergence but alone do not prove correct rounding, a bracket must lie within the same rounding boundaries.
Worked example, certify two decimal places.

The polynomial is continuous, so a root lies strictly inside open bracket one point seven two five, one point seven three five close bracket. Every number there rounds to one point seven three, proving two decimal place accuracy. There is only one positive root because x squared increases for x is greater than zero.
